claims.text: In multiprincipal-element alloys containing moderate-to-high Al and Cr, protective oxide-scale formation is the dominant factor governing oxidation resistance at 800–1200 °C.
Dense, continuous, adherent oxide scales are essential for high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Al and Cr promote formation of thermodynamically stable Al2O3 and Cr2O3 protective scales, respectively.
Protective Al2O3/Cr2O3 scales suppress inward oxygen diffusion and outward metal-cation transport.
Suppression of oxygen and metal transport preserves bulk structural soundness during long-term exposure.
Al and Cr are transported to the alloy surface, where they nucleate and grow dense, adherent Al2O3/Cr2O3 scales.
Increasing Al/Cr content makes the protective scale form more quickly.
Increasing Al/Cr content improves the high-temperature stability of the protective scale.
A stable protective scale reduces internal oxidation.
Optimized-Al/Cr alloys will show lower oxidation mass gain than low-Al/Cr alloys.
Optimized-Al/Cr alloys will develop more continuous protective oxide layers than low-Al/Cr alloys.
Optimized-Al/Cr alloys will develop thicker protective oxide layers than low-Al/Cr alloys.
Optimized-Al/Cr alloys will exhibit less scale spallation and cracking during cyclic oxidation.
A low-Al/Cr baseline forms discontinuous or multilayer, less-stable scales and consequently has greater mass gain and spallation.
The proposed mechanism applies to polycrystalline Al- and Cr-containing multiprincipal-element alloys over 800–1200 °C and extended exposure times.
Outside the stated range, additional-element phases, volatile species, or mechanical loading may govern degradation.
The optimal Al/Cr ratio depends on the other alloying elements and service environment.
Three sets containing 5, 10, and 15 at.% each of Al and Cr, together with a low-Al/Cr reference, can provide a controlled oxidation comparison.
A lack of significant association between Al/Cr content and oxide composition, scale microstructure, or mass-change behavior would falsify the hypothesis.
